practiceQuestions.q: In which year was the comprehensive New Economic Policy (NEP), introducing Liberalisation, Privatisation, and Globalisation (LPG), officially launched in India?
practiceQuestions.sol: The New Economic Policy containing the LPG strategy was introduced in July 1991 by the then Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh to tackle the severe Balance of Payments (BoP) crisis. [Primary Reference: Economic Survey of India / Ministry of Finance archives]

practiceQuestions.q: Who was the Finance Minister of India when the landmark structural reforms of 1991 were presented in Parliament?
practiceQuestions.sol: Dr. Manmohan Singh served as the Union Minister of Finance from 1991 to 1996 and architected the structural adjustment program and macroeconomic stabilization measures. [Primary Reference: Union Budget Speeches, Ministry of Finance]

practiceQuestions.q: The system of 'License-Permit-Quota Raj' which was dismantled under Liberalisation primarily governed which sector of the economy?
practiceQuestions.sol: The License-Permit-Quota Raj restricted industrial growth through extensive bureaucratic controls, capacity licensing, and production quotas, which were largely abolished by the Industrial Policy of 1991. [Primary Reference: Statement of Industrial Policy, 1991, Government of India]

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following best defines 'Privatisation' in the context of the 1991 economic reforms?
opts: Transfer of ownership or management of public sector enterprises to private entities
Imposition of strict price controls on private manufacturing
Restriction of foreign capital inflow into domestic industries
practiceQuestions.sol: Privatisation involves the withdrawal of the state from owning or managing public sector enterprises (PSUs), either through outright sale or disinvestment of equity to private players. [Primary Reference: Department of Public Enterprises, Ministry of Finance]

practiceQuestions.q: What does 'Globalisation' primarily entail in the framework of the 1991 Indian economic reforms?
opts: Isolation of the domestic economy from international trade shocks
Integration of the domestic economy with the world economy through trade, capital, and technology flows
Establishment of regional trade pacts excluding Western nations
Compulsory adoption of a single global currency
practiceQuestions.sol: Globalisation refers to the integration of the national economy with the global economy by removing barriers to foreign trade, lowering tariffs, and encouraging foreign direct investment (FDI) and financial capital mobility. [Primary Reference: Economic Survey, Ministry of Finance]

practiceQuestions.q: In 1991, India faced an acute Balance of Payments (BoP) crisis. Foreign exchange reserves plummeted to a level sufficient to finance imports for roughly how many weeks?
practiceQuestions.sol: By June 1991, India's foreign exchange reserves had depleted to about $1.1 billion, barely enough to cover roughly two weeks of essential imports, forcing emergency gold pledging and IMF bailouts. [Primary Reference: RBI History and Annual Reports]

practiceQuestions.q: Which international financial institutions provided emergency structural adjustment loans to India during the 1991 economic crisis?
opts: Asian Development Bank and New Development Bank
practiceQuestions.sol: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank extended emergency financial assistance conditional on India undertaking sweeping stabilization and structural reform measures (LPG). [Primary Reference: IMF Archives / Ministry of Finance]

practiceQuestions.q: What was a major monetary policy measure undertaken in July 1991 to resolve the BoP crisis prior to structural reforms?
opts: Devaluation of the Indian Rupee against major foreign currencies
Fixing the exchange rate permanently to the US Dollar
practiceQuestions.sol: In July 1991, the Reserve Bank of India undertook a two-step devaluation of the Rupee (by about 9% and 11%) to make Indian exports more competitive and curb excessive imports. [Primary Reference: RBI Bulletin / Economic Survey]

practiceQuestions.q: Under the Industrial Policy of 1991, how many industries were kept under compulsory licensing?
practiceQuestions.sol: The New Industrial Policy of 1991 abolished industrial licensing for almost all industries, restricting compulsory licensing to only 18 industries (subsequently pruned down to 4, primarily relating to security, strategic, and environmental concerns like atomic energy, hazardous chemicals, etc.). [Primary Reference: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade - DPIIT]

practiceQuestions.q: Which statutory body was established in 1992 to protect investor interests and regulate the capital markets, gaining statutory powers as part of financial sector reforms?
practiceQuestions.sol: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) was given statutory powers through the SEBI Act, 1992, to regulate the vibrant capital markets that expanded with financial liberalisation. [Primary Reference: SEBI Act, 1992 / Ministry of Finance]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the 1991 liberalisation reforms alter the character of India's foreign trade policy regarding quantitative restrictions and peak tariffs?
opts: By increasing peak customs duties and banning consumer goods imports entirely
By drastically reducing peak customs tariffs and progressively phasing out quantitative import restrictions (QRs)
By introducing state trading monopolies for all export-import transactions
By pegging import quotas strictly to domestic agricultural output
practiceQuestions.sol: A cornerstone of globalisation and liberalisation was trade reform: peak tariff rates were lowered down from over 300% pre-1991, and quantitative restrictions (QRs) on imports were dismantled (culminating in 2001 following WTO dispute rulings). [Primary Reference: WTO Trade Policy Review on India / Ministry of Commerce and Industry]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the structural rationale behind replacing the MRTP Act (Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act) with the Competition Act, 2002?
opts: To restrict corporate mergers and limit the size of private firms to pre-1991 levels
To shift focus from curbing mere 'bigness' (monopoly control) to preventing anti-competitive practices and promoting market efficiency
To abolish private enterprise and bring all heavy industries under state licensing
To nationalise foreign institutional investors operating in Indian stock exchanges
practiceQuestions.sol: The MRTP Act was designed in a socialist era to curb large asset sizes (bigness per se). In a globalised economy, scale and size are essential for global competitiveness; hence, the Competition Act was enacted to target anti-competitive behavior, cartels, and abuse of dominance rather than size alone. [Primary Reference: Raghavan Committee Report / Competition Commission of India]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the 1991 reforms impact Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) regulations in India?
opts: Complete ban on foreign equity participation exceeding 10% in any sector
Introduction of automatic approval routes for FDI up to specified limits in high-priority industries
Mandatory majority government stake in all foreign joint ventures
Prohibition of profit repatriation by foreign multinational corporations
practiceQuestions.sol: The 1991 reforms replaced bureaucratic discretionary approvals with automatic routes for FDI (initially up to 51% equity in 34 high-priority industries), signalling a welcoming stance toward global capital. [Primary Reference: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) FDI Policy Circulars]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the primary objective behind introducing the 'Navratna' and 'Maharatna' status frameworks for Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs)?
opts: To liquidate loss-making PSUs without offering compensation to workers
To grant enhanced financial and operational autonomy to high-performing PSUs to compete globally
To convert profit-making PSUs into fully government-funded welfare departments
To privatise all public banks overnight
practiceQuestions.sol: To improve PSU efficiency amidst market competition, the government introduced the Navratna (1997) and subsequently Maharatna schemes, giving board-level directors greater financial autonomy for capital expenditure and joint ventures without government clearance up to certain thresholds. [Primary Reference: Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) Guidelines]

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following describes the shift in India's exchange rate regime post-1991?
opts: Fixed exchange rate pegged solely to the British Pound
Transition from fixed peg to a market-determined exchange rate system (Managed Floating)
Adoption of a strictly fixed cryptocurrency standard
Complete abolition of foreign exchange regulations
practiceQuestions.sol: Following the 1991 reforms, India moved away from a pegged exchange rate regime to a market-determined exchange rate system where the value of the Rupee is determined by market forces of demand and supply, with RBI intervening only to curb excessive volatility (Managed Float). [Primary Reference: RBI Reports on Currency and Finance]

practiceQuestions.q: How did financial sector reforms transform the banking sector following the recommendations of the Narasimham Committee (1991)?
opts: By increasing Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) and Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) to maximum historical limits
By reducing pre-emption of funds through lowering SLR/CRR, introducing prudential norms (income recognition and asset classification), and allowing private sector banks
By prohibiting foreign banks from opening branches in India
By nationalising all remaining cooperative banks
practiceQuestions.sol: The Narasimham Committee recommended lowering high SLR and CRR rates that starved banks of lendable resources, introducing capital adequacy norms (Basel standards), and permitting new private banks to foster competition and efficiency. [Primary Reference: Narasimham Committee Report on Financial System, 1991]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the significance of replacing FERA (Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973) with FEMA (Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999)?
opts: Shift from criminal regulation of foreign exchange violations to civil management and facilitation of external trade and payments
Total ban on citizens holding foreign currency accounts abroad
Re-imposition of rigorous export-import licensing controls
Elimination of RBI's oversight over cross-border capital transactions
practiceQuestions.sol: FERA treated every foreign exchange violation as a criminal offense with draconian penalties and presumption of guilt. Aligned with globalisation, FEMA recast foreign exchange laws as a civil statute designed to facilitate external trade and payments and promote orderly foreign exchange markets. [Primary Reference: FEMA Act, 1999 / Ministry of Finance]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the 1991 LPG reforms influence regional disparities and economic federalism in India?
opts: They ensured equal industrial growth across all states simultaneously
They led to market-driven investments favoring states with better infrastructure and institutional capacity, sometimes widening inter-state disparities
They concentrated all foreign investment exclusively in land-locked agrarian states
practiceQuestions.sol: With the dismantling of industrial licensing (which previously directed industrial locations to backward areas via quotas), private capital gravitated toward states with superior infrastructure, skilled labor, and pro-business governance, resulting in divergent growth trajectories among states. [Primary Reference: NITI Aayog Reports / Academic Economic Studies on Regional Convergence]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the impact of trade liberalisation on domestic manufacturing enterprises accustomed to the sheltered 'License Raj' environment?
opts: All domestic firms immediately became global export giants without restructuring
They faced intense competitive pressure from cheap imports and foreign multinational corporations, forcing technological modernization, consolidation, or exit
They were insulated from competition through permanent import bans
They experienced zero efficiency gains due to state subsidies
practiceQuestions.sol: Exposing protected domestic industries to global competition compelled Indian firms to upgrade technology, improve quality, cut costs, and restructure operations, though some uncompetitive units shut down. [Primary Reference: Economic Survey / Reserve Bank of India research papers]

practiceQuestions.q: Which term describes the deliberate sale of minority equity stakes of Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) to the public and institutional investors, introduced as part of privatisation reforms?
practiceQuestions.sol: Minority disinvestment involves the government selling a portion of its equity (typically less than 50%, retaining management control) in PSUs to raise non-inflationary budgetary resources and promote wider public shareholding, as opposed to strategic sale which transfers management control. [Primary Reference: Department of Investment and Public Asset Management - DIPAM]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the economic crisis of 1991 and the genesis of the LPG reforms:
1. The immediate trigger for the 1991 crisis was an unsustainable fiscal deficit coupled with an acute balance of payments crisis triggered by the Gulf War spike in oil prices.
2. Prior to the 1991 policy announcement, India had already maintained a fully convertible capital account for the Rupee since independence.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: The 1991 crisis stemmed from mounting fiscal deficits, foreign exchange depletion worsened by the Gulf War (higher oil import bills and remittance loss from West Asia). Statement 2 is incorrect: India's capital account was heavily restricted under foreign exchange controls (FERA); full capital account convertibility has still not been achieved (Tarapore Committee outlined roadmaps). [Primary Reference: Economic Survey / RBI Reports]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Liberalisation measures in the Industrial Sector (1991):
1. Industrial licensing was completely abolished for all sectors without exception, including hazardous chemicals and defense aerospace.
2. Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) limits on asset sizes of large business houses were removed to encourage corporate growth and expansion.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is incorrect because compulsory licensing was retained for a small negative list of industries (such as defense, explosives, hazardous chemicals, and atomic energy). Statement 2 is correct: Prior clearance requirements under the MRTP Act for capacity expansion or mergers were abolished by repealing the pre-approval sections for large firms. [Primary Reference: Statement of Industrial Policy, 1991 / DPIIT]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Privatisation and Disinvestment process in India:
1. The Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM) functions under the Ministry of Finance.
2. Strategic disinvestment implies the sale of 100% government equity in a PSU along with the transfer of management control to the strategic partner.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: DIPAM (formerly Department of Disinvestment) is a department under the Ministry of Finance. Statement 2 is incorrect because strategic disinvestment involves sale of a substantial portion of government shareholding (not necessarily 100%, often 50% or more) along with transfer of management control. [Primary Reference: Allocation of Business Rules, Cabinet Secretariat / DIPAM]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Globalisation and External Sector reforms in India:
1. The introduction of current account convertibility under Article VIII of the IMF Articles of Agreement in 1994 marked a major milestone for global integration.
2. Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) and Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) were completely barred from investing in Indian equity markets post-1991.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: India accepted Article VIII obligations of the IMF in August 1994, committing to current account convertibility (freedom to convert domestic currency into foreign currency for current international transactions like trade and services). Statement 2 is incorrect: Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) were specifically invited and permitted to invest in Indian capital markets starting from September 1991. [Primary Reference: RBI Annual Reports / IMF Country Reports]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Tax Reforms initiated as part of the 1991 structural adjustment:
1. The Tax Reforms Committee chaired by Chelliah recommended rationalisation of direct and indirect taxes, lowering tax rates, and widening the tax base.
2. Customs duties were significantly increased across all categories to protect domestic manufacturers from external competition permanently.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: The Raja J. Chelliah Committee on Tax Reforms laid the groundwork for modernizing India's tax system by lowering peak tax rates, reducing compliance burdens, and boosting compliance. Statement 2 is incorrect because customs duties were drastically reduced (not increased) to integrate India with global trade and lower input costs for manufacturing. [Primary Reference: Tax Reforms Committee Report, Ministry of Finance]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the criticisms and socio-economic impacts of the LPG strategy in India:
1. Critics argue that LPG reforms have led to jobless growth, agrarian distress, and widening income inequalities between urban and rural sectors.
2. The reforms successfully eliminated all forms of poverty and regional disparities within the first decade of implementation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: While LPG generated high GDP growth and service sector expansion, critics point to concerns regarding inadequate employment generation in manufacturing ('jobless growth'), neglect of agriculture, and rising inequality. Statement 2 is incorrect: Poverty and regional disparities persisted for decades, requiring targeted welfare schemes alongside market reforms. [Primary Reference: Economic Survey / Planning Commission/NITI Aayog Poverty Estimates]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999:
1. FEMA replaced the draconian Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA) to facilitate external trade and promote orderly foreign exchange markets.
2. Under FEMA, all offences related to foreign exchange violations are classified as cognizable criminal offences carrying mandatory imprisonment.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: FEMA was enacted to transition from criminal penalization of forex transactions to civil management. Statement 2 is incorrect: Unlike FERA (which treated violations as criminal offences), FEMA treats violations as civil offences carrying monetary penalties rather than mandatory imprisonment. [Primary Reference: FEMA Act, 1999 / Enforcement Directorate Guidelines]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the evolution of India's Foreign Trade Policy (FTP) in the post-1991 era:
1. The Exim Policy of 1992–97 virtually abolished import licensing, introducing the negative list where items were either freely importable, restricted, or prohibited.
2. Special Economic Zones (SEZs) in India were governed primarily by state-level municipal bye-laws without any central legislation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: The 1992 Exim Policy removed discretionary licensing and streamlined trade under a negative list framework. Statement 2 is incorrect: SEZs in India are governed by a comprehensive central legislation, namely the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, along with its corresponding rules. [Primary Reference: SEZ Act, 2005 / Ministry of Commerce and Industry]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the role of NITI Aayog vis-à-vis economic planning in post-LPG India:
1. NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission to act as a 'think tank' adopting a cooperative federalism approach rather than top-down resource allocation.
2. NITI Aayog possesses the constitutional power to allocate budgetary grants and central plan assistance to state governments.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: NITI Aayog (established in 2015) replaced the Planning Commission, transitioning from centralized planning to cooperative federalism and acting as a premier policy think tank. Statement 2 is incorrect: Unlike the erstwhile Planning Commission, NITI Aayog has no financial allocation powers; fund allocation is handled by the Ministry of Finance and the 15th Finance Commission. [Primary Reference: Cabinet Resolution, Government of India / NITI Aayog charter]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the impact of LPG reforms on the Indian services sector:
1. The services sector (IT, telecommunications, financial services) experienced exponential growth and became the dominant contributor to India's Gross Value Added (GVA).
2. Foreign Direct Investment restrictions on the telecommunications and IT sectors were kept permanently closed even after 1991.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: Liberalisation and globalisation catalyzed the Indian IT and services revolution, making services the largest sector of the Indian economy. Statement 2 is incorrect: Telecommunications and IT sectors were progressively opened up to private and foreign investment (with FDI caps raised up to 100% in telecom over time) to spur technological diffusion. [Primary Reference: National Accounts Statistics, MoSPI / Economic Survey]
